why-ductless-is-the-way-to-go.content:
You deserve the most comfort at the best price in your Arizona home or business. You want reliable heating, ventilation, and air conditioning (HVAC) at reasonable prices. You want fresh, clean air so you and your loved ones can enjoy a healthy home.

Try going ductless.

A ductless system, or mini split, adds comfort to your home without the hassle of having to extend your ductwork. For new construction, additions, retrofits, and remodeling projects, a ductless system is your perfect heating and cooling solution.

At Bucksworth Services, we offer whole-house solutions that help you get the most out of your HVAC investment while adding value to your Arizona home. We believe you should have complete control when it comes to your indoor comfort, safety, and health.

Why Go Ductless?

Air ducts play a vital role in conventional heating and cooling systems—those ducts deliver the goods! But over time, tears and leaks develop in your ductwork that compromise efficiency. The US Department of Energy (DOE) estimates leaky ducts can add hundreds of dollars per year to your heating and cooling costs.

Most experts agree leaky ducts allow up to 25 percent or more of your energy to escape. A ductless system eliminates this type of energy loss.

How a Ductless Mini Split Works

There are two main parts to a mini split: an outdoor condenser and one or more indoor mounted units (additionally, there is the conduit connecting the outdoor and indoor components). A few small holes and tubing are required to connect the outside refrigerant lines to the indoor units.

Our professionals at Bucksworth Services can select the right mini split system to fit your needs and budget, and install it with minimal disruption to your home or office.

With a ductless mini split system, you enjoy the benefits of a zone control system without the ductwork since each interior unit has its own programmable thermostat.

Advantages With a Ductless System

A ductless system uses a washable filter instead of a disposable filter, which is used in traditional systems. Best practice involves cleaning the filter frequently—at least once a month, and more so if you have pets or smokers in your home. Annual maintenance tune-ups and inspections will help extend the life of your system and ensure it runs at full capacity when you need it most.

why-do-i-need-ac-maintenance-now.title: Why Do I Need AC Maintenance Now?
why-do-i-need-ac-maintenance-now.content:
An air conditioner (AC), just like a car, needs regular maintenance and service to run efficiently.

At Bucksworth Services, we recommend getting your air conditioning unit serviced and cleaned at least once a year. The optimum time is in the spring to ensure your system will run with the most efficiency during the hottest summer months. You need to be able to rely on your air conditioner for your comfort here in Arizona.

Why Is Maintenance Important?

The short answer is it saves you money!

Your air conditioner collects dust and dirt continuously as it sits throughout the year here in Arizona, not only in the months when it’s running. Though this tiny debris may not seem harmful, when it accumulates throughout the year, it can make its way into the cracks and crevices of your unit, as well as everywhere else. This creates gunk and wreaks havoc on the different parts involved in the cooling process.

When this happens, parts break down much sooner than expected and can add up to costly repairs. It also decreases the life expectancy of your heating, ventilation, and air conditioning (HVAC) system, forcing you to purchase a new air conditioner much sooner than you may have planned.

Regular air conditioning maintenance also supports your system’s energy efficiency. Simple acts you can perform yourself, like replacing a dirty and clogged air filter, can reduce your energy consumption by 5 to 15 percent, according to the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE).

This translates to you spending less money on your utility bills. Professional and DIY maintenance alleviates higher bills and keeps your air conditioner working at its manufacturer’s intended efficiency.

Even if you are fastidious with doing your own regular home maintenance, you should always have your unit cleaned and checked in the spring by one of our professionals (if not more throughout the year).

There are many tasks only a professional technician is trained and certified to perform. Neglecting these professional tasks constitutes poor maintenance and will negatively affect your system in the long run, again, costing you money. This typically also voids your system’s manufacturer warranty.

What Can I Expect My Technician to Do During My Regular Maintenance?

Here’s a brief overview of what our knowledgeable and experienced technicians do during your air conditioning maintenance appointment:

    • Clean and check condenser coils and evaporators, if necessary.

    • Clean and adjust blower components for proper system airflow to create increased comfort levels.

    • Check ducts for debris, and if debris is present, remove it to allow for maximum airflow.

    • Clean and check aluminum fins. If they are crushed or bent in any fashion, this affects proper air distribution.

    • Inspect internal parts for broken, chipped, or other damage, which may not be easily noticed. If your air conditioner continues to run with damaged parts or areas, your system will eventually fail.

    • Clean and check condensate drain, to prevent any blockages or mold buildup. Backups can cause water damage to equipment.

    • Tighten connections, both mechanical and electrical. Loose connections cause incorrect operations.

    • Check coolant level for leaks. Leaks prevent your air conditioner from working, and the refrigerant could damage anything it touches.

    • Check system’s thermostat for accuracy.

    • Check system controls to be sure all work safely.

    • Provide you with a summary of work performed and share any findings regarding needed repairs or upgrades, as well as maintenance you can perform yourself between maintenance visits.

Schedule Your Maintenance Today

what-does-an-hvac-maintenance-inspection.title: What Does an HVAC Maintenance Inspection Include? Full Checklist
what-does-an-hvac-maintenance-inspection.content:
A professional HVAC maintenance inspection is the single best thing you can do to extend your system's life, lower energy bills, and avoid emergency breakdowns — especially in Arizona where your AC runs 6+ months per year. But what exactly should a technician check? Here's the complete breakdown so you know you're getting a thorough inspection every time.

At Bucksworth Home Services, our Arizona-licensed HVAC specialists follow industry standards from the Air Conditioning Contractors of America (ACCA) on every visit. We serve Phoenix, Tucson, and 33 surrounding cities with transparent, thorough maintenance. Here's what you should expect.

Why Regular HVAC Inspections Matter

Your heating, ventilation, and air conditioning system works harder in Arizona than almost anywhere in the country. Summer temperatures above 110°F mean your AC runs 12–16 hours daily. Without regular maintenance:

  • Energy bills increase 5–15% per year as efficiency degrades
  • System lifespan drops from 15–20 years to as few as 8–10 years
  • Breakdowns happen at the worst times — during peak heat when repair companies are busiest
  • Most manufacturer warranties require documented annual maintenance

According to the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE), an AC with a clean filter uses up to 15% less energy than one with a dirty filter. A full inspection goes far beyond the filter.

Complete HVAC Inspection Checklist

A professional maintenance visit should take 45 minutes to one hour. Anything significantly shorter likely means components were skipped. Here's what a thorough AC inspection and heating check covers:

Component What the Tech Checks Why It Matters
Air FilterCondition, size, MERV ratingDirty filters restrict airflow and increase energy use 5–15%
ThermostatCalibration, programming, responsivenessIncorrect calibration can cause short cycling and uneven temps
Electrical ConnectionsTighten connections, measure voltage/amperageLoose connections cause unsafe operation and component failure

What Happens During an AC Inspection (Step by Step)

Here's the typical flow of a professional HVAC maintenance inspection:

1. Thermostat and Controls Check

The technician verifies your thermostat is calibrated correctly, checks programming settings, and ensures the system cycles on and off properly. They'll also test the system in both heating and cooling modes if applicable.

2. Electrical System Inspection

All electrical connections are inspected and tightened. The tech measures voltage and amperage on motors and compressors, tests capacitors with a multimeter, and checks the contactor for wear. Faulty electrical components are the leading cause of AC failures in extreme heat.

3. Refrigerant System Check

Using gauges, the technician measures refrigerant pressures to confirm proper charge. They inspect refrigerant lines for damage and check for leaks using electronic leak detectors or UV dye. Low refrigerant doesn't just reduce cooling — it can destroy your compressor, the most expensive component in the system.

4. Airflow and Ductwork Assessment

The blower motor and wheel are inspected and cleaned. The tech checks static pressure to evaluate airflow. Visible ductwork is inspected for leaks, disconnections, and damaged insulation. In Arizona, duct leaks in unconditioned attic spaces can waste up to 30% of your cooling.

5. Coil Cleaning and Inspection

Both the indoor evaporator coil and outdoor condenser coil are inspected. The outdoor coil is cleaned to remove dust, debris, and palo verde seed pods (a common Arizona issue). Dirty coils are one of the top efficiency killers.

6. Condensate Drain Service

The drain line is cleared, the drain pan is inspected, and the float safety switch is tested. In humid monsoon months, algae and mineral buildup can clog drain lines and cause water damage to ceilings and walls.

7. Safety and Performance Testing

The tech runs the full system and measures supply and return air temperatures (the "split" should be 15–20°F for cooling). All safety switches are tested. Any carbon monoxide risks from gas furnaces are checked during heating season.

Questions to Ask Your HVAC Contractor

Not all maintenance visits are created equal. Ask these questions to ensure you're getting a quality inspection:

  • Are you licensed, bonded, and insured? — This is non-negotiable. Bucksworth holds Arizona ROC License #343924.
  • Do you follow ACCA standards? — The ACCA sets forth specific checklists by equipment type that quality contractors follow.
  • How long will the inspection take? — Under 30 minutes is a red flag. Thorough maintenance requires 45–60 minutes.
  • What did you find? — Your technician should always be transparent about findings, from minor issues to urgent safety concerns. At Bucksworth, we provide a written report after every visit.
  • What maintenance can I do between visits? — A good tech will explain filter changes (every 30–90 days), keeping the outdoor unit clear, and indoor air quality basics.

Benefits of an HVAC Maintenance Plan

Signing up for a maintenance plan delivers consistent protection and added perks:

  • Longer system life — well-maintained systems last 15–20 years vs. 8–10 for neglected ones
  • Lower utility bills — clean, tuned systems run 10–25% more efficiently
  • Fewer emergency repairs — catch small issues before they become expensive breakdowns
  • Priority scheduling — get faster service during peak summer demand
  • Warranty protection — most manufacturers require documented maintenance
  • Exclusive discounts — Bucksworth plan members get discounts on repairs and new equipment

Bucksworth Home Services makes maintenance simple with automatic appointment reminders, priority service, and member discounts. Get in touch to learn more.

Frequently Asked Questions

How often should HVAC be inspected?

In Arizona, we recommend twice per year — once in spring before cooling season and once in fall before heating season. If you have an older system (10+ years), more frequent checks help catch developing issues early.

How much does an HVAC inspection cost in Phoenix?

A standard AC tune-up in the Phoenix area typically costs $79–$149. Many companies, including Bucksworth, offer maintenance plans that reduce per-visit costs and include additional benefits like priority scheduling and repair discounts.

Is HVAC maintenance really worth it?

Absolutely. The DOE estimates that regular maintenance can reduce heating and cooling costs by up to 15%. More importantly, it prevents surprise breakdowns — the average AC repair in Arizona costs $300–$800, and compressor replacement can exceed $2,000.

What's the difference between HVAC maintenance and HVAC repair?

Maintenance is preventive — it's the routine checkup that keeps your system running well. Repair is reactive — fixing something that's already broken. Regular maintenance dramatically reduces the need for repairs.

Can I do HVAC maintenance myself?

Homeowners should change air filters every 30–90 days, keep the outdoor condenser clear of debris, and ensure vents aren't blocked. However, electrical testing, refrigerant checks, and coil cleaning require professional tools and training. Schedule professional maintenance for these tasks.

what-to-know-about-carbon-monoxide-poiso.content:
Carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning is known as the silent killer for a reason—it can easily go undetected and cause illness and even death. It’s critical to learn how to prevent carbon monoxide leaks in your Surprise home—as well as what the symptoms of carbon monoxide poisoning are in case you are exposed.

Bucksworth Services has all the answers to your carbon monoxide questions. You can trust our team to provide you the information you need to remain safe from dangers like carbon monoxide leaks.

What Is Carbon Monoxide and How Could I Be Exposed to It Inside My Home?

Carbon monoxide is an odorless and colorless gas. It is released when something is burned—so your boiler, furnace, water heater, car, grill, dryer, fireplace, chimney, and many other household appliances could be a source.

You may experience a carbon monoxide leak as a result of fuel failing to burn completely or even by leaving your car running for an extended period in an enclosed space like your garage.

What Are the Symptoms of Carbon Monoxide Poisoning?

Exposure to carbon monoxide prevents oxygen from reaching your tissues and organs, ultimately depriving your body of it. The higher the levels of carbon monoxide in the air and the longer your exposure to it, the more severe the outcome can be.

According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), unintentional carbon monoxide poisoning is responsible for 400 deaths, 20,000 emergency room visits, and 4,000 hospitalizations in the United States each year.

How Can I Reduce the Risk of Carbon Monoxide Poisoning?

Using home appliances and systems as designed, in addition to taking proper care of them by opting for routine maintenance, can help you reduce the risk of carbon monoxide forming and leaking into your home.

You can also install carbon monoxide detectors throughout your home. An alarm will go off and promptly inform you when carbon monoxide is present, allowing you to get out of your home before further exposure and call for help.

Other ways to prevent exposure to carbon monoxide include:

  • Installing, repairing, and maintaining all major appliances properly.
  • Routinely inspecting and performing safety checks on your heating, ventilation, and air conditioning (HVAC) system and water heater.
  • Using generators, camping stoves, and gas or charcoal grills outside only and away from doors or windows leading to your home.
  • Never leaving your vehicle running in the garage—even if the garage door is open.
  • Never using a gas oven for heat or burning anything in your stove or fireplace without proper ventilation.

9-signs-of-bug-infestation-in-your-home.title: 9 Signs of a Bug Infestation in Your Home (And What to Do Next)
9-signs-of-bug-infestation-in-your-home.content:
Spotting one bug doesn't necessarily mean you have an infestation — but spotting the right warning signs early can save you thousands in property damage and protect your family's health. Arizona homes are especially vulnerable because our warm, dry climate supports year-round pest activity from scorpions, cockroaches, termites, and dozens of other insects.

Here are the nine most reliable signs of a bug infestation in your home and what each one tells you about the type of pest you're dealing with.

Why Bug Infestations Are Dangerous

Bugs aren't just unpleasant — they pose real health and safety risks. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC):

  • Mosquitoes, ticks, and fleas can transmit malaria, Zika, West Nile, Lyme disease, and plague
  • Cockroaches trigger asthma attacks and allergic reactions, especially in children
  • Bed bugs cause intense itching that can lead to secondary infections
  • Termites cause over $5 billion in property damage annually in the U.S.

Recognizing infestation signs early and taking action is critical. Here's what to look for.

1. Wood Shavings and Sawdust Piles

Likely pest: Carpenter ants or termites

Fine wood shavings (called "frass") near baseboards, window sills, or door frames signal wood-boring insects. Carpenter ants push shavings out of their galleries as they tunnel through your home's structure. Unlike termites, carpenter ants don't eat the wood — but the structural damage is just as serious.

What to do: Don't disturb the shavings. Call a licensed pest control professional to identify the species and assess structural damage. Carpenter ant and termite treatments are very different.

2. Mud Tubes and Discarded Wings

Likely pest: Subterranean termites

Pencil-width mud tubes running along your foundation, garage walls, or plumbing pipes are a hallmark of subterranean termites. These tubes protect termites as they travel between their underground colony and your home's wood. You may also find piles of tiny, translucent wings near windows and doors after a termite swarm.

What to do: Schedule an immediate termite inspection. Termites work silently — by the time you see visible signs, damage may already be significant.

3. Buzzing Sounds in Walls or Attic

Likely pest: Bees, wasps, or roof rats

A persistent buzzing, humming, or scratching sound from inside walls, your attic, or chimney often indicates a hidden colony. In Arizona, Africanized honey bees commonly build hives in wall voids, attic spaces, and irrigation valve boxes. If you notice many bees entering and exiting a specific spot on your home's exterior, a hive is likely established inside.

What to do: Never attempt to remove a bee hive yourself — Africanized bees are aggressive when disturbed. Contact a licensed pest control or bee removal specialist immediately.

4. Rust-Colored Stains and Tiny Eggs on Bedding

Likely pest: Bed bugs

Bed bugs leave telltale evidence on mattresses, box springs, and upholstered furniture: small rust or reddish-brown blood stains, tiny white eggs (about the size of a pinhead), pale yellow shed skins, and live bugs hiding in seams and crevices. Bites typically appear as itchy, red welts in a line or cluster.

What to do: Inspect mattress seams, headboard joints, and nearby furniture with a flashlight. Wash all bedding in hot water (130°F+). Professional heat treatment is the most effective elimination method.

5. Metallic Bugs in Damp Areas

Likely pest: Silverfish

These torpedo-shaped, silvery insects love dark, humid spaces — bathrooms, basements, laundry rooms, and under kitchen sinks. Silverfish feed on paper, glue, textiles, and starchy foods. Finding more than one or two indoors suggests a breeding population hidden nearby.

What to do: Reduce moisture with exhaust fans and dehumidifiers. Store paper goods and textiles in sealed containers. Treat baseboards and entry points with residual insecticide or call for professional treatment.

6. Droppings That Look Like Ground Pepper

Likely pest: Cockroaches

Cockroach droppings resemble ground black pepper or coffee grounds. You'll find them behind appliances, inside cabinets, under sinks, and near water sources. Seeing just one cockroach typically means dozens — or hundreds — are hiding nearby. Egg cases (oothecae) look like small, dark brown capsules.

What to do: Deep clean affected areas. Seal gaps around plumbing penetrations. Eliminate moisture sources. For established infestations, professional bait and treatment programs are far more effective than store-bought sprays.

Pepper-like droppingsCockroaches🟡 High — health risk
Spider webs + egg sacsSpiders🟢 Moderate — monitor

Maggots near trashFly larvae🟡 High — infestation imminent

7. Webs, Egg Sacs, and Multiple Spider Sightings

Likely pest: Spiders (including black widows)

Spiders are natural pest controllers — they eat flies, mosquitoes, and crickets. But multiple spider sightings in one day, visible webs in corners and closets, and small white egg sacs indicate a population that's growing beyond control. In Arizona, black widow and brown recluse spiders pose genuine health risks.

What to do: Clear clutter that provides hiding spots. Reduce outdoor lighting that attracts their prey insects. Seal cracks around windows and doors. If you spot black widows, contact a professional — their bites require medical attention.

8. Swarms of Flies That Won't Go Away

Likely pest: House flies, drain flies, or fruit flies

A few flies slipping through an open door is normal. Persistent swarms mean a breeding source exists — often decaying organic matter, clogged drains, overripe fruit, or an animal that died in a wall void or attic. House flies carry over 100 disease-causing pathogens on their bodies.

What to do: Find and eliminate the breeding source. Clean drains with enzyme cleaners. Empty trash daily. If flies persist despite cleaning, a dead animal in the structure may be the cause — call for professional inspection.

9. Maggots Near Trash or Outdoor Areas

Likely pest: Fly larvae (imminent infestation)

Maggots — small, white, worm-like fly larvae — near garbage cans, pet areas, or compost bins mean flies are actively breeding on your property. Left unchecked, a few maggots can turn into hundreds of adult flies within days.

What to do: Clean the affected area thoroughly with boiling water or a bleach solution. Secure trash in lidded containers. Move outdoor garbage cans away from entry doors. Treat the area with residual insecticide to break the breeding cycle.

Bonus: Watch for Millipedes Near Your Foundation

Woodpiles, mulch, leaf piles, and decorative rock within 12 inches of your foundation create perfect habitat for millipedes. These many-legged arthropods enter through foundation cracks, gaps under doors, and window openings. While not dangerous, large numbers indicate excess moisture — which also attracts far worse pests like cockroaches and termites.

When One Bug Means Many More

For some pests, seeing even one is cause for concern:

  • One cockroach = likely dozens hiding nearby (they're nocturnal — daytime sightings mean overcrowding)
  • One bark scorpion = likely more in your walls and attic (they travel in clusters)
  • One termite swarm = an established colony has been feeding on your home for months or years
  • One bed bug = check immediately; they reproduce rapidly (a female lays 1–5 eggs per day)

Frequently Asked Questions

How do I know if I have a bug infestation or just a few bugs?

Occasional sightings of a single bug near a door or window are usually incidental. An infestation is indicated by multiple sightings, droppings, egg cases, structural damage, or persistent activity in the same area. If you're seeing bugs daily or finding evidence like droppings or shed skins, it's time to call a professional.

What are the most common bug infestations in Arizona?

Cockroaches (especially German and American roaches), bark scorpions, ants (fire ants and carpenter ants), termites, and bed bugs are the most common infestations in Phoenix and Tucson homes. During monsoon season, crickets and mosquitoes spike significantly.

Can a bug infestation make you sick?

Yes. Cockroach allergens trigger asthma attacks (especially in children), mosquitoes and ticks transmit serious diseases, bed bug bites can cause secondary infections from scratching, and fly infestations spread over 100 pathogens. Prompt treatment is both a comfort and health issue.

Should I try to treat a bug infestation myself?

Minor ant trails and occasional spiders can often be managed with store-bought products and prevention measures. However, infestations involving termites, scorpions, bed bugs, or established cockroach populations require professional treatment. DIY approaches for these pests typically waste time and money while the infestation grows.

Whoever named the heat pump was being modest.

Not only do heat pumps generate heat, but they can also pump out cool air. What’s more, a new heat pump can cut your Arizona energy costs by up to 50 percent when you make the switch from a furnace or baseboard heater, according to the US Department of Energy (DOE).

In some ways, heat pumps have an edge over the traditional combination of a furnace and central air conditioning (AC) unit. Air Conditioners vs. Heat Pumps

From our desk, here’s how heat pumps compare to a conventional HVAC system:

Cooling Capabilities

During warm weather, heat pumps work identically to a central AC system. Both units extract heat and humidity from the air, sending it to the condensate drain.

Heating Capabilities

AC units have no heating function. During the winter, your AC goes on standby, and the furnace takes the reins. Furnaces generate heat through combustion, burning natural gas, or oil. On the other hand, heat pumps harvest heat from the air and pressurize it in high concentrations. They transfer energy rather than generate it.

Geography

Homeowners living in colder climates tend to favor furnaces that can create lots of heat no matter how cold it is. Heat pumps rely on heat already in the air—they operate less effectively in subfreezing temperatures.

In regions with cold winters, we recommend combining a heat pump with a furnace to create a dual fuel system. This can still be somewhat more efficient than relying on a furnace alone but largely depends on the number of subfreezing days in that region per year.

Environmental Impact

As we mentioned before, heat pumps can double your energy efficiency. It also means you’ll see a substantial drop in your monthly utility costs. To enjoy even more cost savings, consider purchasing a geothermal heat pump, the greenest heating and cooling system on the market. Using energy it naturally extracts from below the ground, the geothermal heat pump heats and cools your home, using only minimal amounts of electricity.

Carbon Monoxide (CO) Risk

Gas furnaces rely on combustion to produce heat. For this reason, there is a small chance of CO leak without regular cleaning and inspection. Heat pumps use no combustion, therefore eliminating the possibility. Regardless, you should have CO detectors installed in every room, and keep up with routine maintenance.

how-does-an-air-conditioner-work.content:
As a homeowner here in Arizona, it’s always a good idea to learn as much as you can about your appliances. That means knowing their basic operations, what features are included, and if any necessary upkeep is involved. Needless to say, this is no exception for your air conditioning (AC) unit.

How It All Began

The modern air conditioner is designed to transfer cool air throughout your home to keep you comfortable during the year’s hottest months. This marvel was originally invented in 1902 by Willis Haviland Carrier. He developed the air conditioner to solve a humidity problem at a printing plant in Brooklyn, New York, and was ultimately credited with creating a system of chilled coils to maintain a constant temperature.

Today, the Energy Information Administration (EIA) reports that 87 percent of homes in the United States use air conditioners and account for nearly 12 percent of total energy costs each year. That’s why we at Bucksworth Services in Phoenix & Tucson want you to know all about your cooling system and what it takes for your trusted investment to keep running efficiently for years to come.

How It Works

As a consumer, it’s important to understand the key elements of your cooling system, and that starts with knowing your air conditioner’s five main functional components and how they work together:

1. Compressor—the key to refrigerant conversion

Working like a pump inside your unit, this is often considered the “heart” or “engine” of your air conditioner. The compressor is located in the outdoor portion of your system, which is referred to as the condenser. Once the system is activated by your thermostat, the compressor starts to pull in a low-temperature, low-pressure refrigerant in gas form from your system. The gas is then compressed to a higher pressure and temperature before being released to the condenser coil.

2. Condenser—outdoor coil

The condenser coil is also located in the outdoor portion or your system. It’s made up of a piping sequence with thousands of small fins on it. The refrigerant runs through this coil after exiting the compressor. A fan pulls outside air across the coil to remove the heat from the refrigerant with the assistance of the fins for maximum heat dispersement. This process causes the refrigerant to convert back to a high-pressure liquid state prior to entering the expansion valve.

3. Expansion valve—mechanical component regulating refrigerant

This critical part of the system is responsible for controlling the conversion and amount of refrigerant passed through to the evaporator. This is typically located on the indoor portion of your system. High-pressure liquid refrigerant is forced through a small orifice in the valve that causes the pressure reduction as it passes through. The refrigerant expands to a liquid/vapor mix at this point that’s allowed to enter the evaporator coil.

4. Evaporator—indoor coil

The evaporator is a series of piping creating another coil that the liquid/vapor refrigerant passes through and absorbs the heat from the air passing over it. This lowers the temperature of the air that is then distributed throughout your home by way of its ductwork, lowering the temperature throughout the space. The cycle continues when the refrigerant makes its way back to the compressor to keep the air in your home regulated to the desired temperature setting on your thermostat.

5. Blower—indoor fan

The blower is a fan that pulls warm air through the air filter in the return ductwork. It pushes that air over the evaporator coil to be distributed via your ductwork throughout your home.

In addition to cooling your home, an air conditioner can also help address humidity in your home by humidifying and dehumidifying. Some units include a moisture collection pan that absorbs the moisture from the air as the refrigerant absorbs heat.

That bad thing is, well, they are spiders. Pests. Creepy, crawly arachnids that are not exactly welcome guests in your home. The black widow spider and Arizona recluse spider even pose a potential health problem if they bite you.

One spider in your home is a nuisance and easily remedied. More than a few can disrupt your daily routine.

You do not want to spend the day on spider patrol, searching every nook and cranny with a rolled-up magazine or vacuum hose in hand. There are better ways to regain peace of mind and control of your Phoenix home.

How Do I Get Rid of Spiders?

Spiders can enter your home through holes in window and door screens, cracks in your home’s foundation, gaps around doors and windows, vents, and pipes. You can carry them inside on items you have left outdoors, such as firewood, plants, and laundry.

Some may have grown up in your home. They may have been living under your furniture, in storage boxes in the attic, or behind the laundry area in your moist basement for a long time, feeding on bugs and becoming more visible when they are out and about looking to mate or for prey.

Keeping Spiders Out

Repair cracks in the foundation of your home. Replace worn weatherstripping and caulk around doors and windows. Fix torn window screens. Attach door sweeps to the bottom of storm doors to create a tight seal that keeps pests out. Be sure the dryer vent damper closes when the appliance is off.

Keep firewood away from your home and trim shrubs and trees away from your home’s siding or roof. Use a broom to brush away spider webs.

Tips to Get Rid of Ants

  • Target the source: Ants gravitate toward sources of food and water. If you eliminate the source, the ants will eventually be on their way. Clean your table after eating and remove any crumbs. Wash your dishes and utensils, or place them in the dishwasher—but don’t leave them sitting in your sink, especially if they are not rinsed and have leftover food on them.
  • If you have pets, don’t forget to clean their water bowl regularly. Check for other common water sources, like condensation in your bathtub or showers and leaky pipes. Clean your bathroom and fix your pipes so water doesn’t continue to appear and entice the ants.
  • Clean your countertops, kitchen table, and bathrooms: Keep your home clean. Even though ants can still infest well-kept homes, cleaning your home can deter them, especially if you use soap which is known to repel ants.
  • Cleaning with vinegar is a good idea too. Vinegar is a natural cleaning agent, but it also repels and kills ants too.
  • Get rid of the ants with basic household items: Mix dish soap and water, and then use the mixture as a spray to kill the ants.
  • Ants are irritated by the smell of pepper so you can sprinkle ground black or red pepper near any ant trails to keep them away. Mixing pepper with water and spraying it on the ants is another effective way to kill the ants.

  • Buy an ant spray to use: You could always purchase an over-the-counter ant spray. Ant sprays kill ants on the spot, and there are also sprays you can use that will kill the ants when they appear in the area you sprayed.
  • You could spray the perimeter of your home, the entrances of your home, and certain problem areas inside your home where the ants are found the most.
  • Keep them out by caulking and weatherstripping: Be sure to prevent the ants from getting inside your home in the first place. Look to see where the ants are coming from. Weatherstrip holes, tears, or crevices between your windows or doors to keep out the ants.
  • Check to see if there are areas in the walls where the ants are entering, and close them up by using caulk or foam insulation for larger cracks and holes.

a-guide-to-handling-and-preventing-summe.title: A Guide To Handling and Preventing Summer Pest Infestations
a-guide-to-handling-and-preventing-summe.content:
Arizona’s hot summer weather means there is often a huge amount of pest activity inside and outside of houses and commercial buildings. The monsoon season makes pests an even bigger problem, since heavy rains can drive some of them out of their underground nests and into buildings. Rain also provides insects and other pests with the water they need to survive and reproduce. Discover the most common types of pest infestations in Phoenix and Tucson and find out how to prevent and overcome them.

Ants

When spring arrives in Arizona, the common ant species become more active, because of the emergence of new queens who are ready to establish their own nests. They are even more active throughout the monsoon season. Some ant species are merely a nuisance, but species like carpenter ants and fire ants can be a much bigger problem.

Carpenter ants are attracted to wood since they make their nests by boring through the wood and using all the pieces as nesting materials. Like termites, carpenter ants have the potential to do major damage to buildings, since they often end up nesting and boring tons of holes in wooden joists and studs.

While the primary habitat of the two most prevalent fire ant species in Arizona is the outdoors, there are instances where they can be found in places like sheds and detached garages. The main issue with a fire ant infestation is that they are extremely aggressive and prone to biting to defend themselves. Their bites are also excruciating and can even potentially result in death if the ants swarm or the person is allergic, with elderly people and infants being at the highest risk.

Forelius ants and sugar or pavement ants are two of the species most likely to infest homes since they often come inside in search of food. These species won’t cause damage, but they are still unsanitary and something you want to get taken care of.

The best way to prevent ant infestations inside a building is to make sure you keep everything clean and don’t leave any food sitting out. Using lids on your trash cans also helps to prevent the ants from having access to a food source. Keeping the outside of the building clean and making sure there are no sources of wood near the building helps to avoid issues with carpenter ants. When dealing with any type of ant infestation, you normally won’t be able to get rid of the infestation yourself.

The infestation will often worsen over time as well, which is why it’s you should contact a professional pest control company at the first sign of an infestation. It’s also important to seal up any potential access points in the exterior structure of your building to stop ants and other pests from getting inside.

Cockroaches

Cockroaches are one of the most common pest problems in Arizona. As with ants, they are attracted to dirty environments and any sources of food. Some species will just occasionally get inside but prefer living outside, while others prefer to nest and live inside buildings where they have steady access to food and water. If you see a few cockroaches inside, many others are likely present as well. If you don’t hire a pest control company to deal with the problem and eliminate entry points, you’ll almost certainly end up with more and more of them inside as they can reproduce quickly.

Termites

Termites are one of the worst pests because of the extensive structural damage they can cause. Avoiding wood and vegetation near the building deters pests. Once they get inside, the only way to get rid of them is with professional termite control. If you suspect your building has termites, it’s important to act fast to limit the amount of damage they can cause. If you want to detect a termite infestation, keep an eye out for signs such as holes present in wood, window and door frames, sheetrock, or even windows and doors that are difficult to open. Additionally, the presence of insect wings can also be an indication of a termite problem. Another sure sign of a termite issue is if you see mud tubes in the ground near the building since these tubes lead to subterranean termite nests.

Scorpions

It is common to find scorpions under potted plants, woodpiles, and other places where they have shelter. The reason that they’re often attracted to buildings is because of potential sources of water. Keeping the area around the building clean and eliminating sources of water and shelter can help to keep scorpions away. If you already have them nesting around your building or you see multiple scorpions inside, it’s time for professional pest control. That’s because the only way you can usually get rid of them is by using insecticide. Another issue is that the reason scorpions may live inside your building is that of other types of pests that the scorpions are feeding on. If you consistently observe scorpions indoors, it implies the potential existence of multiple infestation types.

Mosquitoes

Mosquito eggs and larvae can only survive in water. That’s why it’s important to check around your property regularly, ensuring there is no standing water inside buckets, birdbaths, or anywhere else. Adult mosquitoes seek shelter in tall grass and weeds, which is why you need to keep your lawn trimmed short and your property free of weeds. Unfortunately, there’s often nothing you can ever do on your own to keep mosquitoes away from your property. If you have a constant influx of them swarming around outside or getting inside, the best and only effective solution is with a mosquito lawn treatment. This type of treatment will eliminate any mosquitoes and keep them returning for up to a month.

preparing-your-home-for-pest-season-a-se.title: Seasonal Pest Control Checklist for Arizona Homeowners | 2025 Guide
preparing-your-home-for-pest-season-a-se.content:
Arizona homeowners face a year-round battle with pests — from bark scorpions emerging in spring to rodents seeking warmth in winter. A seasonal pest control checklist keeps you one step ahead of infestations before they start. At Bucksworth Home Services, we've helped thousands of Phoenix and Tucson families stay pest-free with preventive strategies tailored to our desert climate.

Whether you handle prevention yourself or schedule professional pest control services, this month-by-month checklist ensures nothing slips through the cracks.

Why Arizona Needs a Seasonal Pest Control Plan

Unlike cooler climates where winter freezes kill off most insects, Arizona's mild winters let pests remain active all year. Scorpions, termites, roaches, and rodents simply shift behavior patterns with the seasons rather than dying off. That's why a one-time treatment rarely works — you need a seasonal pest control checklist that adapts to what's active each quarter.

Season Top Arizona Pests Priority Action
Spring (Mar–May)Termites, scorpions, carpenter beesSeal entry points, schedule termite inspection
Summer (Jun–Aug)Mosquitoes, ants, roaches, fliesEliminate standing water, secure food storage
Fall (Sep–Nov)Rodents, stink bugs, spidersSeal gaps, store firewood away from home
Winter (Dec–Feb)Cockroaches, spiders, bed bugsReduce indoor moisture, deep clean

Spring Pest Prevention Checklist (March–May)

Termite swarming season kicks off in spring across the Phoenix metro, and carpenter bees begin boring into wooden structures. Queen bees emerge from dormancy to build new colonies near homes. Scorpions become more active as temperatures rise above 70°F.

Seal Entry Points

Walk the perimeter of your home and inspect for gaps around pipes, utility lines, and the foundation. Use caulk, weatherstripping, or expanding foam to close openings. Even a gap as small as 1/16 of an inch is wide enough for a scorpion to squeeze through.

Clear Foundation Debris

Remove fallen branches, leaf piles, and mulch within 12 inches of your foundation. These materials trap moisture and create ideal hiding spots for scorpions, crickets, and roaches.

Trim Vegetation

Keep trees, shrubs, and landscaping at least 6–12 inches away from your home's exterior walls. Overhanging branches are highways for ants, roof rats, and spiders to access your roof and attic.

Inspect Screens and Weatherstripping

Replace torn window and door screens. Check weatherstripping around all exterior doors — if you can see daylight, pests can get in. This is one of the most cost-effective steps on any pest prevention checklist.

Schedule a Termite Inspection

Spring is the best time for a professional termite inspection. Look for discarded wings near windows, mud tubes along the foundation, and hollow-sounding wood.

Summer Pest Prevention Checklist (June–August)

Summer in Arizona means monsoon moisture, which drives mosquitoes, ants, and cockroaches into overdrive. Temperatures above 100°F push pests indoors seeking water and cooler shelter.

Eliminate Standing Water

Drain birdbaths, empty plant saucers, and clear blocked gutters after monsoon rains. Mosquitoes can breed in as little as a bottle cap of stagnant water. Walk your property weekly during monsoon season.

Secure Food Storage

Store pantry items in airtight containers. Clean up spills immediately, especially outdoors during barbecues. Never leave pet food out overnight — it's a magnet for roaches and rodents.

Repair Plumbing Leaks

Fix dripping faucets and running toilets promptly. In the desert, any moisture source attracts pests from a wide radius. Check under sinks, around water heaters, and near plumbing connections.

Use Yellow "Bug Lights" Outdoors

Replace standard porch lights with yellow or sodium vapor bulbs that are less attractive to flying insects. Position lights away from doors and windows to avoid drawing bugs toward entry points.

Maintain Lawn and Garden

Mow regularly, remove weeds, and trim back ground cover. Overgrown yards provide shelter and breeding grounds for crickets, spiders, and invasive weeds that attract additional pests.

Fall Pest Prevention Checklist (September–November)

As desert temperatures cool, rodents like pack rats and roof rats seek shelter inside homes. Spiders become more visible as males wander in search of mates, and stink bugs look for warm overwintering sites.

Seal Cracks and Gaps (Again)

Re-inspect your home's exterior — summer heat can cause caulk to crack and weatherstripping to deteriorate. Pay extra attention to areas around utility penetrations, dryer vents, and where the roof meets the wall.

Store Firewood Properly

Keep firewood stacked at least 20 feet from your home and elevated off the ground. Woodpiles are prime habitat for bark scorpions, black widows, and termites.

Clean Chimneys and Dryer Vents

Have chimneys professionally cleaned and inspected. Install caps or screens to prevent birds, roof rats, and bats from nesting inside. Don't forget dryer vents — lint buildup attracts pests and creates a fire hazard.

Inspect Attics and Crawl Spaces

Look for rodent droppings, chewed wiring, nesting materials, or gaps that could admit pests. Ensure proper ventilation to prevent moisture buildup that attracts cockroaches and silverfish.

Clean Gutters

Clear leaves and debris from gutters before winter. Clogged gutters create moisture near your roofline — an invitation for mosquitoes, wasps, and wood-damaging pests.

Winter Pest Prevention Checklist (December–February)

Arizona winters are mild, but nighttime lows in the 30s–40s drive cockroaches, spiders, and even scorpions indoors. Holiday travel can also introduce bed bugs from hotels.

Plug Small Gaps with Steel Wool

Fill gaps around pipes and utility penetrations with steel wool, then seal with caulk. Rodents can't chew through steel wool, making it more effective than foam alone.

Reduce Indoor Moisture

Use exhaust fans in bathrooms and kitchens. Consider a dehumidifier for basements, attics, and crawl spaces. Low humidity makes your home less inviting to cockroaches, silverfish, and centipedes.

Inspect Insulation

Check attic and wall insulation for signs of rodent damage — shredded material, droppings, or urine stains. Replace contaminated insulation and seal entry points discovered.

Deep Clean Your Home

Declutter storage areas, vacuum behind appliances, and clean under sinks. Fewer hiding spots and food crumbs mean fewer pests surviving the winter indoors.

Inspect Holiday Items

Before bringing holiday decorations from storage or luggage from travel, inspect for pests. Bed bugs, spiders, and roaches can hide in boxes, suitcases, and fabric items.

Month-by-Month Quick Reference

Month Key Tasks
JanuaryCheck for rodent activity, inspect insulation
FebruaryRe-caulk exterior gaps, clean storage areas
MarchStart perimeter pest treatments, schedule termite inspection
AprilTrim vegetation, check screens and doors
MayBegin scorpion prevention, seal A/C line penetrations

SeptemberRe-seal exterior, begin fall rodent prevention

When to Call a Professional

DIY prevention goes a long way, but some situations require professional intervention:

  • Active termite signs — mud tubes, discarded wings, or hollow wood
  • Scorpion sightings — seeing even one bark scorpion indoors suggests more are hiding
  • Rodent droppings — especially in kitchens, pantries, or near food storage
  • Recurring roach problems — if DIY sprays aren't controlling the population
  • Bee or wasp nests — never attempt removal yourself, especially Africanized bee hives

Living in Arizona means air conditioning isn’t a luxury, it’s a necessity. But keeping your home cool during the long, hot summer months can send your energy bills soaring. The good news? You don’t have to sacrifice comfort to save money. With a few simple changes and regular upkeep, you can improve your AC efficiency and lower your cooling costs without breaking a sweat.

At Bucksworth Home Services, we understand the unique demands of Arizona’s desert climate. Whether you’re in Phoenix or Tucson, these practical, expert-backed tips will help you get the most out of your air conditioning system, keeping your home cool and your budget in check.

1. Schedule Regular HVAC Maintenance

Your AC system works hard, especially during our triple-digit summers. Without regular maintenance, dirt and wear can drag down performance and increase your utility bill. A yearly tune-up from a licensed HVAC technician ensures your unit runs efficiently and helps prevent costly breakdowns when you need cooling the most.

During a maintenance visit, our Bucksworth pros will:

  • Clean or replace air filters
  • Check refrigerant levels
  • Inspect electrical components

  • Clear out debris and dust

Routine service not only improves efficiency but can also extend the lifespan of your system.

2. Change Air Filters Frequently

One of the simplest, and most effective, ways to improve AC efficiency is by changing your air filter regularly. A clogged or dirty filter restricts airflow, forcing your system to work harder and use more energy.

Arizona tip: With all the desert dust and pollen in the air, we recommend checking your filter monthly and replacing it at least every 1-3 months.

3. Seal and Insulate Your Home

If your cool air is leaking out, your AC has to work overtime to maintain the temperature. Sealing gaps around windows, doors, and ductwork keeps the cool air in and the hot air out.

Consider:

  • Using weather stripping or caulking on windows and doors
  • Insulating your attic and walls
  • Having your ductwork inspected and sealed if needed

Proper insulation is especially important in Arizona homes, where the attic can reach extreme temperatures. Bucksworth offers expert insulation services to help you maintain a consistent indoor temperature year-round.

4. Install a Programmable Thermostat

Smart thermostats allow you to control your home’s temperature more precisely, and even remotely. You can set it to raise the temperature when you’re away and cool things down before you return.

A small change like setting your thermostat to 78°F when you’re home and 85°F when you’re away can make a big difference. According to the U.S. Department of Energy, this adjustment can save you up to 10% annually on cooling costs.

5. Use Ceiling Fans Strategically

Ceiling fans don’t lower the room temperature, but they do create a wind-chill effect that makes you feel cooler. When used in conjunction with your AC, they allow you to raise your thermostat a few degrees without sacrificing comfort.

Important: Make sure your fans are spinning counterclockwise in summer to push cool air down.

6. Keep Sunlight Out During Peak Hours

In Arizona, the sun can quickly heat up your home, especially through south- and west-facing windows. To reduce heat gain:

  • Close blinds and curtains during the hottest parts of the day
  • Install solar screens or window film
  • Plant shade trees or use outdoor awnings for additional protection

These small adjustments reduce the load on your AC and help keep indoor temperatures more stable.

7. Avoid Heat Buildup from Appliances

Ovens, stoves, and even some lighting can add extra heat to your home. Try these tips:

  • Cook outside on the grill during the hottest months
  • Use a microwave or slow cooker instead of the oven
  • Run the dishwasher and clothes dryer in the evening or early morning

Reducing indoor heat sources keeps your home cooler and eases the burden on your AC.

8. Upgrade an Older AC Unit

If your air conditioner is more than 10–15 years old, it may be time to consider a replacement. Modern systems are significantly more energy-efficient, especially those with high SEER (Seasonal Energy Efficiency Ratio) ratings.

Though it’s a larger upfront investment, a new system can lead to substantial long-term savings on your energy bills, not to mention improved comfort and reliability. Our Bucksworth HVAC specialists can help you choose the right unit for your home and budget.

Strange noises, inconsistent cooling, or rising energy bills could be signs your system is struggling. Addressing issues early can prevent bigger (and more expensive) problems down the road.

the-dangers-of-ignoring-termite-damage-i.content:
Older homes hold character, history, and charm that newer properties often lack. Yet they are also more vulnerable to pests, particularly termites. Termite damage may not be immediately visible, but over time, it can compromise the safety, structure, and value of a property. In older houses, ignoring these issues creates far-reaching consequences that no homeowner should overlook.

Unlike modern builds that use treated lumber or advanced construction methods, many older houses rely on original wood materials that termites find especially attractive. Years of natural wear and exposure can make beams, flooring, and framing even more susceptible to infestations. This combination of age and hidden activity is why termite damage in older homes should never be underestimated.

Arizona Termite Species That Target Older Homes

Arizona is home to several termite species, but two pose the greatest threat to older houses in the Phoenix and Tucson metro areas. Understanding which species you are dealing with determines the treatment approach and urgency of action.

Species Behavior Damage Pattern Risk to Older Homes
Subterranean Termites Build mud tubes from soil to wood; need ground contact Attack from the bottom up — foundation, floor joists, subfloor Extreme — older foundations have more entry points
Drywood Termites Live entirely inside wood; no soil contact needed Target exposed wood — attic framing, window frames, eaves High — original wood in older homes lacks modern treatment
Desert Dampwood Require moisture; target water-damaged wood Focus on plumbing areas, leaky roofs, irrigation-adjacent walls Moderate — older plumbing increases moisture risk

In the Phoenix metro, subterranean termites account for the vast majority of structural damage. Older homes built before the 1990s often lack the pre-treated soil barriers that modern construction requires, making them significantly more vulnerable. If your home was built before 1995, a professional termite inspection is not optional — it is essential.

Structural Weakness That Grows Over Time

Termites feed silently, targeting wood and other cellulose-based materials that serve as the backbone of a home. In older houses, where wood may already show signs of wear, its impact accelerates deterioration. Small, hidden infestations can escalate into significant structural issues if left unchecked.

Key structural risks include:

  • Hollowed beams that weaken load-bearing walls 
  • Compromised flooring that begins to sag or creak under pressure 
  • Roof damage where the wood framing is directly attacked 
  • Doors and windows that no longer align due to shifting support

These problems rarely appear suddenly. They develop gradually, making them harder to notice until repairs become extensive and costly. Regular inspections help homeowners detect termite damage before it evolves into a safety hazard.

Hidden Costs Beyond Repair Work

While structural repairs are expensive, the financial burden of ignoring termite activity extends further. Older houses are particularly vulnerable because damage often spreads undetected until it has impacted multiple areas. The longer termites remain active, the higher the expenses climb.

Additional financial consequences include:

Stage of Damage Typical Repair Cost What Is Involved
Early detection (1-2 years) $500 – $1,500 Spot treatment, minor wood replacement

Safety Hazards for Residents

Beyond financial and structural concerns, termite damage creates safety risks that directly affect those living in older houses. Weakened wood framing and hidden voids increase the chance of accidents or emergencies that could have been prevented with timely intervention.

Safety hazards include:

  • Collapsing floorboards that give way under everyday use 
  • Roof instability that heightens the risk of leaks or collapse 
  • Weakened staircases and decks that can suddenly fail 
  • Walls that bow or crack due to compromised support beams

These issues not only threaten the physical integrity of the house but also endanger everyone inside. Addressing termite damage early preserves not just the structure but also the well-being of its occupants.

Warning Signs of Termite Damage in Older Arizona Homes

Termites work silently, but they leave evidence if you know where to look. In older homes, these signs are often mistaken for normal aging or settling:

  • Mud tubes along foundation walls, garage walls, or in crawl spaces — the signature of subterranean termites
  • Hollow-sounding wood when tapped — healthy wood produces a solid thud; infested wood sounds papery
  • Buckling or blistering paint on walls, door frames, or window sills — moisture from termite activity pushes paint outward
  • Frass (termite droppings) — small pellets resembling sawdust near baseboards or window ledges indicate drywood termites
  • Doors and windows that suddenly stick — termite damage warps wood framing, changing how openings align
  • Swarmers or discarded wings near windows in spring — termite swarm season in Arizona runs March through May
  • Sagging floors or ceilings — advanced structural damage that demands immediate professional attention

Long-Term Impacts on Historical Value

For many owners, older houses hold sentimental and historical significance. Preserving their original features is part of their appeal. Termite damage threatens these qualities, eroding the craftsmanship that defines older homes. Decorative woodwork, antique floors, and original framing are often the first to suffer.

Once this damage occurs, restoration rarely returns the home to its authentic state. Replacement materials cannot fully capture the original workmanship, reducing the cultural and historical value of the property. Ignoring termites not only diminishes function but also erases the very details that make an older house special.

Older homes face unique vulnerabilities that termites exploit quickly. Left untreated, damage compounds into financial loss, safety hazards, and permanent deterioration. Early detection and professional intervention remain the only effective solutions to preserve both the integrity and value of older houses.

If you suspect termites may be damaging your home, waiting only worsens the outcome. Safeguarding your property’s structure and value begins with expert care and proven solutions.

Frequently Asked Questions About Termite Damage in Older Homes

How quickly can termites destroy an older house?

A mature subterranean termite colony can consume roughly one pound of wood per day. In an older home with untreated wood framing, significant structural damage can develop within 2 to 3 years. However, visible signs often do not appear until damage is already extensive, which is why annual inspections are critical.

Does homeowners insurance cover termite damage in Arizona?

No. Standard homeowners insurance policies in Arizona do not cover termite damage. Insurance companies classify termite infestations as a preventable maintenance issue. This means the full cost of repairs falls on the homeowner, making prevention and early detection the only financial protection.

Should I get a termite inspection before buying an older home?

Absolutely. Arizona lenders often require a Wood Destroying Organism (WDO) inspection before approving a mortgage on older properties. Even if your lender does not require it, an independent termite inspection can save you from inheriting thousands of dollars in hidden damage.

For most older homes in the Phoenix and Tucson areas, a combination of liquid barrier treatment around the foundation and targeted spot treatment for active colonies delivers the best results. Baiting systems can supplement this approach for ongoing monitoring. The right solution depends on the species, severity, and construction of your specific home.

How often should older homes be inspected for termites?

We recommend annual inspections for any Arizona home over 20 years old. Homes with previous termite history or those near irrigation, mature trees, or desert washes should be inspected every 6 to 12 months. Learn more about how Arizona's climate affects termite activity.

Scorpions are among the most resilient pests in Arizona, thriving in the hot desert landscape and often making their way into residential neighborhoods. For Phoenix homeowners, dealing with a scorpion infestation can feel overwhelming, especially because these pests are highly skilled at remaining hidden until their population grows. Spotting the earliest indicators is essential for preventing larger problems and protecting your household. Below are the most telling signs that scorpions may be present in your home, along with insights into why detection should never be delayed.

Nighttime Sightings Indoors and Outdoors

Scorpions prefer the dark, becoming most active once the sun sets. Unlike many pests that scatter under bright lights, scorpions are adapted to nighttime activity, making evening hours the best time to catch a glimpse of them. Even so, a sighting of one or two scorpions does not necessarily mean the problem is small. In fact, a single sighting can point to a broader scorpion infestation that remains hidden in cracks, crevices, or shaded areas of the yard.

Homeowners often notice them:

  • Along baseboards, walls, or ceilings inside living spaces 
  • In bathrooms, laundry rooms, and kitchens, where water is accessible 
  • Around outdoor patios, gardens, or stone landscaping after dark

Some residents use blacklights at night to identify their faint glow, which comes from a substance in their exoskeletons. While this may confirm activity, it also reveals how easily scorpions conceal themselves during the day. If you find them repeatedly in the same areas, it often signals they have established reliable hiding places both indoors and outdoors.

Presence of Shed Exoskeletons

Like other arachnids, scorpions grow by shedding their outer shells. These exoskeletons are dry, translucent, and often curled, making them difficult to spot at first glance. However, their presence is one of the clearest signs of an ongoing scorpion infestation, since multiple molts occur before a scorpion reaches maturity.

Common areas where exoskeletons are discovered include:

Scorpion exoskeletons are more than just a byproduct of growth. They also suggest that scorpions are thriving in a location with food and shelter. Because Phoenix homes often provide dark corners and a steady insect population, scorpions are likely to return and reproduce unless their environment is altered. Careful inspection of low-traffic areas is key to spotting these subtle warning signs early.

Unexplained Sting Incidents

Perhaps the most distressing evidence of scorpion activity is the sting itself. Arizona is home to the bark scorpion, the most venomous species in the United States. While not always life-threatening, stings can cause severe pain, numbness, or allergic reactions that require medical attention, especially for young children and older adults.

You may notice:

  • Painful stings while retrieving items from closets or storage 
  • Pets reacting suddenly after exploring dark spaces 
  • Increased tension around beds, couches, or shoes where scorpions may hide

If you notice a surge in crickets, cockroaches, or other insects around your yard or inside your home, chances are high that scorpions are nearby as well.

The presence of multiple hiding spots allows scorpions to establish long-term residency. Since they can survive for years and reproduce steadily, infestations rarely disappear without intervention. A home that provides consistent shelter becomes increasingly attractive to these pests, making proactive detection and professional control essential.

How to Identify Arizona Bark Scorpions

The Arizona bark scorpion (Centruroides sculpturatus) is the most dangerous scorpion species in the United States and the most common scorpion found in Phoenix homes. Identifying them correctly is essential for assessing the threat level of an infestation.

Key identification features include:

  • Size: Adults measure 2 to 3 inches long, making them one of the smaller scorpion species in Arizona
  • Color: Light tan to yellowish-brown, sometimes with faint darker stripes along the back
  • Tail: Thin, elongated tail that curves upward — distinctly slender compared to other species
  • Climbing ability: Unlike most scorpions, bark scorpions can climb walls, ceilings, and rough surfaces with ease
  • Glow: Under UV/blacklight, they fluoresce a bright blue-green, making nighttime detection with a blacklight one of the most effective identification methods

For many homeowners, the first instinct when they discover insects or rodents is to search for quick DIY pest control methods. Hardware stores and online retailers market sprays, traps, and powders that promise fast solutions for infestations. The attraction is understandable: do-it-yourself approaches often seem cheaper, more immediate, and less disruptive than scheduling professional service.

However, what appears simple at first rarely works in practice. Pests are resilient and adapt quickly to surface treatments. While a can of spray may kill the few insects you see, it does not address the hidden colony or entry points that allowed them in. In the meantime, infestations grow larger, often spreading to new areas of the property.

The risks go beyond wasted money. Misusing chemicals can endanger children, pets, and even the environment. Improper handling may also push pests deeper into walls, attics, or crawl spaces, making them harder to eliminate later. The truth is that infestations require more than just a visible solution; they demand an understanding of pest biology, behavior, and environmental factors.

Why DIY Pest Control Fails

The failure of DIY efforts is not due to lack of effort but rather the complexity of pest infestations. Each species requires a different strategy, and success depends on addressing root causes rather than symptoms. Some of the most common reasons why DIY pest control fails include:

  • Superficial treatments only: Sprays or powders kill what you see but leave colonies, nests, or eggs untouched. 
  • Resistance development: Many pests adapt to common chemicals, reducing effectiveness over time. 
  • Incomplete coverage: Infestations often extend into hidden areas that homeowners cannot easily reach. 
  • Health and safety risks: Misapplied products expose families and pets to unnecessary toxins. 
  • Failure to prevent recurrence: Without sealing entry points or addressing conditions that attract pests, infestations return.

These recurring problems highlight why infestations linger even after multiple DIY attempts. For households juggling busy schedules, the repeated expense and frustration of failed efforts can outweigh the upfront cost of professional service.

The Importance of Identifying Root Causes

Successful pest control begins with identifying why an infestation occurred in the first place. Professionals are trained to evaluate environmental conditions that make a home attractive to pests. Moisture, clutter, structural cracks, and unsealed food storage are often underlying factors. DIY solutions rarely address these root causes, focusing instead on visible insects or rodents.

For example, eliminating a trail of ants without locating the colony ensures they will return. Spraying cockroaches seen at night does little when dozens remain hidden during the day. Termite damage may go unnoticed entirely until it becomes severe. Each of these examples illustrates why comprehensive inspection is essential.

fall-pest-inspection-checklist-for-homeo.content:
When the air turns crisp and temperatures drop, pests start searching for warm, protected shelters. Unfortunately, homes offer everything they need: food, warmth, and safety from the elements. A thorough fall pest inspection ensures that your living space remains free of unwanted intruders before the season changes.

Below is a detailed guide from pest control experts outlining how to inspect, identify, and prevent pest problems before they multiply, saving you from costly and unpleasant surprises later.

Exterior Evaluation: Protecting the First Barrier

The best defense against pest intrusion begins outside your home. As autumn sets in, rodents, spiders, and insects look for easy entry points. An exterior assessment helps you stay one step ahead.

Focus on the following during your inspection:

  • Foundation and Walls: Check for small cracks or gaps that ants, beetles, or rodents can squeeze through. Even tiny openings can become entry routes.

  • Windows and Doors: Look for worn seals, broken screens, or loose weather stripping. Replace or repair damaged components to keep pests outside.

  • Roof and Gutters: Remove leaves and debris that trap moisture and attract insects. Clean gutters to ensure proper drainage.

  • Utility Openings: Seal gaps around pipes, vents, and wiring. These small gaps are common rodent access points during fall and winter.

A complete exterior review serves as your first layer of protection. Small improvements here can prevent larger infestations later on.

Interior Inspection: Identifying Hidden Trouble

Once inside, pests settle into quiet corners where they can reproduce undisturbed. Attics, basements, and kitchens are key hiding spots that deserve careful attention during your fall pest inspection.

Check these indoor areas closely:

  • Basements and Crawl Spaces: Control humidity and inspect for water leaks, as damp areas attract centipedes and termites.

  • Attics: Look for droppings, shredded insulation, or gnawed wires, which are common signs of rodent nesting.

  • Plumbing Lines and Vents: Ensure pipes are sealed and condensation is minimal to discourage moisture-loving insects.

Homes with recurring pest activity benefit most from regular professional inspections. Timely detection not only protects against infestations but also safeguards wiring, insulation, and building materials that rodents often destroy.

Moisture and Sanitation: Reducing Pest Attraction

Moisture is a magnet for pests of all kinds, particularly termites, cockroaches, and ants. Managing humidity and sanitation in your home plays a major role in reducing pest attraction.

Focus on these key maintenance points:

  • Fix Leaks: Even minor pipe leaks create ideal conditions for pest survival.

  • Control Humidity: Use dehumidifiers in basements or storage spaces to maintain dry conditions.

  • Clean Regularly: Vacuum and mop floors to eliminate crumbs and organic debris.

  • Empty Trash Properly: Use sealed bins and remove garbage frequently.

  • Check Drainage: Make sure downspouts move water away from foundations to prevent damp soil near entry points.

Clean environments may not guarantee a pest-free home, but they significantly reduce what attracts them in the first place. Combined with seasonal inspections, this preventive care limits the chances of long-term problems.

Seasonal Prevention: Acting Before Pests Move In

A certified professional can also spot early warning signs of termites, rodents, and ants before they escalate. Their precision and experience make them an invaluable partner in protecting both your home and your peace of mind.

how-termites-thrive-in-arizonas-unique-c.title: How Termites Thrive In Arizona’s Unique Climate
how-termites-thrive-in-arizonas-unique-c.content:
Arizona’s desert climate may seem too hot and dry for termites to survive, yet the state is home to some of the most persistent termite populations in the country. Beneath the surface, moisture pockets, landscaping irrigation, and structural materials provide ideal environments for colonies to grow and spread. Termite control in Arizona requires specialized knowledge of local soil conditions, seasonal behavior, and the specific species that have adapted to this region’s challenges.

Understanding why termites thrive in Arizona’s unique climate helps homeowners appreciate the importance of prevention and early detection before damage becomes extensive.

Why Arizona’s Climate Favors Termites

Termites depend on a balance of warmth and moisture, two factors Arizona provides in abundance through its seasonal patterns. The state’s high temperatures accelerate termite activity, while irrigation systems and monsoon rains offer the humidity these pests need to survive.

Several aspects of Arizona’s environment create perfect conditions for colonies to thrive:

  • Warm soil temperatures: The ground rarely cools enough to disrupt termite activity, allowing colonies to remain active year-round.

  • Irrigated landscapes: Moisture from lawns, gardens, and drip systems softens soil and provides drinking sources for subterranean termites.

  • Monsoon season: Heavy summer rainfall creates the humidity termites need for swarming and reproduction.

  • Wood-rich structures: Homes built with wood framing, fences, and decks supply continuous food sources.

Even in arid regions, subterranean termites can burrow deep into the soil, where conditions remain humid enough for survival. Once established, they construct intricate tunnel networks that allow them to reach wooden structures without ever exposing themselves to open air.

Common Termite Species In Arizona

Arizona hosts multiple termite species, each with distinct behaviors and habitat preferences. Recognizing which types are present in your area is crucial for accurate identification and effective termite control.

Here are the most common termite species found across the state:

  • Pest Control in Green Valley: Green Valley Pest Control: Reliable Defense for Your Desert Sanctuary
  • Desert subterranean termites: The most widespread species in Arizona. They prefer sandy soil and are highly active during summer.

  • Arid-land subterranean termites: Known for building deep colonies that can extend under sidewalks and foundations.

  • Western drywood termites: Unlike subterranean species, they live entirely within the wood they consume and require minimal moisture.

  • Dampwood termites: Found in higher elevations and areas with consistent moisture, such as near rivers or irrigated land.

Because each species behaves differently, effective treatment must be tailored to the infestation type. For example, drywood termites require localized treatments, while subterranean species often demand soil-based barrier or bait systems. Neglecting proper identification can result in incomplete treatment and recurring damage, especially in older homes where vulnerabilities and termite damage risks are more common.

Environmental Factors That Support Termite Colonies

While Arizona’s desert landscape may seem hostile, the state’s urban development and irrigation practices have unintentionally created thriving habitats for termites. Colonies often form in the soil beneath homes, feeding on buried wood or structural foundations.

These environmental factors play a key role in termite survival:

  • Moisture sources: Air conditioning condensation, leaky spigots, and sprinkler systems provide steady water access.

  • Soil composition: Sandy or loamy soil is easier for termites to tunnel through compared to rocky terrain.

  • Temperature stability: Termites avoid extreme surface heat by nesting underground, where soil temperatures remain moderate.

  • Urban growth: Construction sites and new housing developments disturb soil, exposing wood debris that attracts termites.

Over time, even small colonies can expand rapidly. Once established, they are difficult to eradicate without specialized equipment and professional expertise. Since infestations often remain hidden, many homeowners only realize the extent of the damage once visible signs appear, such as bubbling paint, hollow wood, or mud tubes along walls.

Why Professional Termite Control Is Essential

Homeowners may try do-it-yourself termite solutions, but these rarely address the root of the problem. Professional termite control involves a deeper understanding of colony biology, environmental triggers, and safe application methods that stop infestations at their source.

Experts use advanced tools and proven strategies that include:

  • Targeted treatments: Depending on the species, professionals use bait systems, soil barriers, or localized treatments.

  • Prevention plans: Regular monitoring ensures that termites do not return after initial treatment.

  • Moisture management: Specialists identify leaks or drainage issues that could encourage future infestations.

Relying solely on over-the-counter products can result in short-term relief without eliminating the colony. These treatments often miss underground nests or internal wood infestations. Preventing Termite Infestations In Arizona Homes

While professional termite control provides the most effective protection, homeowners can take proactive measures to reduce the likelihood of infestation. These preventive habits make properties less appealing to termites and limit access points around foundations.

Practical prevention strategies include:

  • Eliminate moisture sources: Repair leaks, improve drainage, and avoid overwatering landscaped areas near the home.

  • Reduce wood-to-ground contact: Keep wood siding, fences, and mulch several inches above soil level.

  • Inspect regularly: Schedule annual termite inspections to identify early warning signs.

  • Seal entry points: Close gaps around plumbing, utility lines, and foundation cracks.

  • Maintain proper ventilation: Reduce humidity in crawl spaces and attics with dehumidifiers or vents.

Preventive care, when combined with professional maintenance, provides comprehensive protection against Arizona’s resilient termite populations.

Early detection and consistent prevention are essential to avoid expensive structural repairs and maintain long-term home value.
